Scrub Daddy's first offer valued the company at $200K.
The final deal valued it at $1M. The sponge didn't change.

Kevin opened at $100K for 50%. Then Daymond and Lori jumped in, and the price climbed until the founder got exactly his ask: $200K for 20%.

One buyer sets the price. Several buyers fight over it.

That's why serious sell-side advisors run a process: multiple buyers, one deadline.

Would you have taken the first offer?

Kevin offered Scrub Daddy $100K and let the founder keep 100%.
It may have been the most expensive offer in the room.

The structure: 50 cents a sponge until repaid, then 10 cents a sponge forever. At 50M sponges a year, that's $5M a year for one check.

And a royalty that never ends doesn't vanish when you sell. Buyers treat it like debt: they cut the price or make you buy it out first.

Compare offers by total cost over time, not the size of the check.

Would you sign a royalty that never ends? Yes or no.

Four Sharks passed on DoorBot. Kevin offered only a royalty.
The founder walked away. Amazon later bought it, as Ring, for a reported $1B.

Kevin's offer: $700K, 10% of every sale until repaid, then 7% forever.
The counter: a loan with an end date. Kevin said no.

A loan ends. A royalty never does. And every future buyer would have priced that 7% into the deal.

The wrong deal is worse than no deal.

Would you have taken Kevin's royalty to land a deal on TV? Yes or no.

Wicked Good Cupcakes took Kevin's royalty instead of selling equity: 45 cents a jar, forever.
Then Hickory Farms bought the business, and the royalty came with it.

They kept 100% of the company, and it paid off. But a forever royalty is an invisible passenger in every future sale.

A royalty isn't good or bad. It's a cost. Price it before you sign it.

45 cents a jar, forever. Would you sign it? Yes or no.

Bombas asked for $200K for 5%.
They closed at 17.5%, and it may be the best deal in Shark Tank history.

The founders didn't just negotiate valuation. They negotiated what the money would do: a $200K line of credit for inventory.

A product business rarely dies from a low valuation. It dies from running out of cash between buying inventory and getting paid.

Negotiate the working capital, not just the price.

Would you give up 17.5% for inventory financing? Yes or no.

Kevin O'Leary offered $750K for 100% of GrooveBook.
Ten months later, Shutterfly bought it for $14.5M.

The founders didn't sell the company on Shark Tank. They sold 80% of the licensing rights for $150K and kept 100% of the business.

Part of the Shutterfly price was an earn-out: money paid later, only if targets are hit. And in 2022 the buyer shut the product down.

Three lessons for any owner reviewing an offer:
1. Selling a side door is not selling the house.
2. An earn-out is a promise, not cash.
3. After closing, the buyer decides what survives.

Would you have sold the whole company to Kevin for $750K? Yes or no.

All five Sharks invested $1M in Breathometer.
In 2017 the FTC alleged the devices often under-reported blood alcohol. The company settled without admitting the allegations.

The price went up because everyone wanted in. Nobody stopped to ask if the product worked.

In a real acquisition, the buyer doesn't just buy revenue. They inherit every promise the company ever made.

Hype raises the price. It never lowers the risk.

Who should have caught it: the Sharks or the founder?

Mark Cuban offered $30M cash for 100% of Coffee Meets Bagel.
Three times their own valuation. They said no.

Afterward they raised roughly $20M from investors, selling more of the company with every round.

A buyout offer isn't just a number. Weigh it against the risk of the plan, the dilution ahead, and the years it takes to beat it.

Would you have taken Mark's $30M? Yes or no.

Albertsons paid a reported $200M for Plated in 2017, the year Amazon bought Whole Foods.
Two years later: a $38M write-down and the service shut down.

Plated's Shark Tank deal fell apart after the show. The real exit came from timing: a grocer afraid of falling behind.

For sellers: timing is value. Sell into the panic.
For buyers: fear is not a valuation.

Was $200M a smart buy or a panic buy?

Two Sharks wanted 50%+ of Bantam Bagels for $275K.
The founders said no, took Lori's deal, and sold to T. Marzetti for $34M in 2018.

Barbara wanted 51%. Kevin wanted 50%. That's not an investment, it's control.

Then the twist: in 2022 the new owner discontinued the brand. Once you sell, the buyer decides what lives.

Early money is the most expensive money. Never sell control just to get started.

Would you give up 51% to get started? Yes or no.

Every acquisition has two prices: the headline and the net.

Poppi (then Mother Beverage) took $400K for 25% on Shark Tank, a $1.6M valuation. In 2025 PepsiCo agreed to pay $1.95B. PepsiCo also said $300M of that was expected tax benefits, putting the net price at $1.65B.

Two takeaways for owners: the partner can matter more than the valuation, and a headline price needs to be read down to what actually changes hands.

Equity you sell cheap is the most expensive money you will ever raise.

Kodiak Cakes asked $500K for 10% on Shark Tank. The offers implied $1M to $1.4M valuations. The founders declined both, kept 100%, and kept control of when and to whom they would sell. In 2021, L Catterton acquired a majority stake (terms undisclosed) with the founders staying on as minority owners.

Before accepting dilution, model what that stake is worth at the exit.

A purchase price is a stack, not a number.

When Aterian acquired Squatty Potty in 2021, its filings show roughly $30.8M in total consideration: about $19M in cash at closing, about $8M for transition services, and an earn-out of up to about $4M tied to targets. The business had about $16.8M in trailing revenue and $4.7M in operating income.

If you're selling, model each layer: what's guaranteed, what's contingent, and when it's paid.

Financial investors price your cash flow. Strategic buyers price what you do for them.

Rocketbook got zero offers on Shark Tank at a $4M valuation. In 2020, BIC acquired 100% of the company for $40M, a way into digital writing for a pen maker.

Before you go to market, list the buyers who need your product, customers or capability. They are often the ones who pay the premium.

A handshake is the start of a deal, not the end of one.

Notehall shook on $90K for 25% with Barbara Corcoran on Shark Tank, then walked away weeks after the episode aired. In 2011, Chegg acquired the company for $3.7M in equity (per the SEC filing) plus undisclosed cash, and hired both founders.

Until the definitive agreement is signed, both sides still have choices. Plan accordingly.

A dollar in year seven is not a dollar today.

On Shark Tank, Moki Doorstep described a licensing deal guaranteeing $3M over seven years plus a 12.5% royalty, then accepted a $3M offer for 100% of the company. At an illustrative 10% discount rate, $3M paid evenly over seven years is worth about $2.1M today.

When a business's value sits in a contract, discount the cash flows before you set a price.

In any negotiation, how you answer is part of the price.

BedJet's founder pitched strong unit economics on Shark Tank ($98 to make, $499 retail, roughly 80% gross margin before shipping and retailer cuts) but lost the room. No deal. The day after the episode aired, Mattress Firm announced it would carry the product.

Investors price the operator as well as the margin. Retail buyers price the product. Prepare for both.

Equity is the most expensive capital most founders ever raise.

The Lip Bar asked $125K for 20% on Shark Tank and got no offers. Instead, the founder cold-called a Target buyer: Target.com in 2016, Target stores in 2018, and later an announced launch in 3,000 CVS stores.

A retailer buying inventory grows revenue without taking ownership. Run that option before you price your equity.
